subject: business-studies
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What does the term 'e-commerce' mean?
options: Buying and selling goods or services over the internet
Sending business emails to customers
Storing business data on computers
Advertising a business on television
questions.explain: E-commerce is the trading of goods and services electronically, mainly over the internet.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of digital communication used by businesses?
options: Social media
A printed newspaper advert
A billboard poster
A face-to-face meeting
questions.explain: Social media is a form of digital communication allowing businesses to interact with customers online.

questions.q: How can e-commerce benefit a small business?
options: It allows the business to reach a wider, potentially global market
It removes the need to keep any financial records
It guarantees that profits will always increase
It means the business no longer pays any taxes
questions.explain: Selling online removes geographical limits, letting a business reach customers far beyond its local area.

questions.q: A clothing shop introduces a website with online ordering. Which cost is most likely to rise as a direct result?
options: Spending on website maintenance and delivery
The rent on its high-street premises
The wages of its cleaning staff
The cost of its shop fittings
questions.explain: Moving to online selling adds costs such as running the website and delivering orders to customers.

questions.q: What are business ethics?
options: Moral principles that guide how a business behaves
The legal rules a business must follow
The total profit a business makes each year
The marketing methods a business uses
questions.explain: Business ethics are the moral principles influencing decisions about what is right and wrong.

questions.q: Why might acting ethically create a trade-off for a business?
options: Ethical choices can raise costs and reduce short-term profit
Ethical choices always make a business bankrupt
Ethical choices are illegal for most businesses
Ethical choices remove the need to pay suppliers
questions.explain: Behaving ethically, such as paying fair wages, often increases costs, creating a trade-off with profit.

questions.q: Which of the following is an environmental consideration for a business?
options: Reducing pollution and waste from production
Increasing the number of shareholders
Raising the price of its products
Hiring more sales staff
questions.explain: Environmental considerations include limiting pollution, waste and the use of scarce resources.

questions.q: How can a pressure group influence a business's decisions?
options: By campaigning to change how the business behaves
By setting the business's selling prices
By paying the business's corporation tax
By appointing the business's directors
questions.explain: Pressure groups use campaigns and publicity to push businesses towards more ethical or environmental behaviour.

questions.q: A coffee chain switches to fully recyclable cups but charges 10p more per drink. This best shows that ethical decisions can:
options: Involve a trade-off between doing good and higher prices
Guarantee lower costs for the business
Have no effect on customers at all
Break consumer protection law
questions.explain: The more sustainable choice raises costs that are passed on, showing the trade-off between ethics and price.

questions.q: What is inflation?
options: A general rise in the prices of goods and services
A fall in the number of people employed
The total value of a country's exports
The interest charged on a bank loan
questions.explain: Inflation is the sustained general increase in the price level of goods and services over time.

questions.q: What does the interest rate represent?
options: The cost of borrowing money and the reward for saving
The rate at which prices rise each year
The percentage of workers who are unemployed
The tax charged on imported goods
questions.explain: The interest rate is the price of borrowing money and the return earned on savings.

questions.q: What is a likely effect on a business when interest rates rise?
options: Loan repayments become more expensive, reducing spending and investment
The business automatically pays lower wages
Consumer incomes always rise sharply
The business is no longer allowed to borrow
questions.explain: Higher interest rates increase borrowing costs, so both businesses and customers tend to spend and invest less.

questions.q: How does high unemployment in the economy usually affect businesses selling consumer goods?
options: Demand tends to fall as people have less income to spend
Demand always rises because people have more free time
Costs of raw materials automatically fall to zero
The business must legally lower its prices
questions.explain: Unemployment lowers total incomes in the economy, reducing consumer spending and demand for many goods.

questions.q: A furniture retailer sees sales fall after interest rates increase. Which explanation fits best?
options: Customers are borrowing less and delaying big-ticket purchases
The retailer has been forced to raise wages by law
Inflation has fallen to zero
The retailer's exports have become cheaper
questions.explain: Expensive borrowing makes customers postpone large purchases like furniture, reducing the retailer's sales.

questions.q: What is globalisation?
options: The growing integration and interdependence of the world's economies
The closing of a country's borders to all trade
A tax placed only on domestic goods
A fall in the number of multinational companies
questions.explain: Globalisation is the increasing connection between economies through trade, investment and movement of goods and people.

questions.q: What is a tariff?
options: A tax placed on imported goods
A subsidy paid to exporters
A limit on the number of workers a firm can hire
A discount given to loyal customers
questions.explain: A tariff is a tax on imports that raises their price and can protect domestic producers.

questions.q: How can a rise in the value of the pound affect a UK business that exports goods?
options: Its exports become more expensive abroad, so demand may fall
Its exports automatically become cheaper abroad
It no longer has to pay any tariffs
Its imported raw materials become more expensive
questions.explain: A stronger pound raises the foreign price of UK exports, which can reduce overseas demand for them.

questions.q: A UK toy maker imports plastic parts from abroad. If the government raises tariffs on these imports, the most likely result is:
options: The firm's production costs increase
The firm's production costs fall to zero
The firm can no longer sell in the UK
The firm's exports become tariff-free
questions.explain: Higher tariffs on imported components raise the cost of the parts the toy maker buys, increasing its costs.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of employment legislation affecting businesses?
options: The national minimum wage
The rate of inflation
The exchange rate
The level of e-commerce sales
questions.explain: The national minimum wage is employment law setting the lowest hourly pay a business can legally give workers.

questions.q: How does consumer protection legislation, such as the requirement that goods be of satisfactory quality, affect a business?
options: It must ensure products meet legal standards or risk refunds and legal action
It allows the business to sell any quality of goods it wishes
It removes the need to describe products accurately
It means the business pays no tax on sales
questions.explain: Consumer law requires goods to be of satisfactory quality, so businesses must meet standards or face refunds and legal consequences.
